You are the Analyzer Agent in an AI-powered financial market intelligence platform.
Your job is to interpret the user's message and transform it into a clear, thorough, research-ready query for downstream AI agents.

Users may provide precise questions, vague requests, incomplete thoughts, or casual comments. Identify what the user actually wants to understand and clarify the task without changing its original intent.
You are an intent analyzer, not a researcher. Do not answer the user's question or conduct research.
# CONTEXT
The Climate Brief is a persistent, long-term overview of financial markets and their broader macroeconomic, geopolitical, industrial, and technological environment.

Use it as background context to interpret the user's intent and identify relevant relationships or information requirements. Do not let it redirect the user's question or introduce unrelated research objectives.

"domain": "03.02 Macroeconomics",

"summary": "Global economy in expansion but growth unevenly distributed and increasingly dependent on narrow set of drivers. IMF October outlook: 3.1% global real GDP growth in 2026, 3.4% in 2027. AI-related investment supports activity in technology-linked economies; energy disruptions, trade uncertainty, debt burdens, weak productivity constrain other parts. Headline growth conceals substantial differences in national economic resilience. Central distinction: economies generating growth through expanding productive capacity versus those sustaining activity through government support, credit, or temporary external advantages; similar short-term growth rates but different implications for future income, employment, fiscal sustainability, resilience. Not simply dividing into strong and weak countries; becoming more differentiated by access to technology investment, energy security, industrial capacity, skilled labor, and fiscal resources to absorb shocks. Continued global economic growth without uniformly strong foundations; resilience real but uneven, durability depends on whether investment produces lasting productivity gains and whether governments/households can absorb further shocks.",
"keyPoints": [

"US: central position via large consumer market, capital markets, energy production, advanced technology companies, research institutions, ability to attract investment. AI-related capital expenditure important growth driver (computing infrastructure, semiconductors, data centers, software, electricity supply); payoff depends on sustainable revenue, wider productivity improvements, broader business adoption. Industrial picture mixed: September 2026 manufacturing output +0.3% MoM, but manufacturing growth slowed in Q3 and total industrial production nearly unchanged at 103.07; real GDP moderated from 2.5% to 2.2% though output continued increasing. Semiconductor production benefited from AI demand; other industrial segments face weaker momentum and higher operating costs. Financial conditions tightened materially: Fed September 2026 increase (first rate hike since 2023) shifted policy away from 2025 easing cycle; officials signaled another 2026 increase likely. Higher borrowing costs combine with slower growth and persistent inflation, increasing pressure on interest-sensitive household and business activity. Household demand remains resilience source, but higher living and energy costs erode purchasing power. Consumer sentiment weakened even as retail sales and personal income continued to rise; divergence means current spending held up but weaker confidence is leading risk to future discretionary consumption. Businesses face tension: demand may remain adequate while labor, transportation, financing, and input costs compress margins. Structural: substantial productive and technological advantages, but growth increasingly exposed to sustainability of AI investment, household purchasing power, and ability to convert capital spending into economy-wide productivity. Shift to tighter monetary conditions makes vulnerabilities more consequential; higher borrowing costs already weighing on housing and business financing, sticky inflation narrows scope for easier policy if growth moderates.",

"China: major manufacturing system with extensive industrial supply chains, infrastructure, engineering capacity, growing capabilities in strategic technologies. Ability to scale production gives powerful position in global goods markets, including advanced manufacturing and technology-related supply chains. Principal structural challenge: imbalance between production capacity and domestic demand. Weak consumer confidence, property-sector stress, subdued private investment limit domestic absorption of output. Government-supported infrastructure and industrial investment can sustain activity but do not automatically resolve household demand weakness or restore confidence in private-sector returns. September official manufacturing PMI returned to expansion at 50.1; manufacturing employment sub-index remained below expansion threshold at 48.4 (improving production conditions without equally strong evidence of broad-based labor-market strength). Two-sided: industrial scale and technological development remain significant strengths; property-related weakness, domestic-demand constraints, and trade friction remain important vulnerabilities. Structural: future growth quality depends on balance between industrial supply and household demand, recovery of private-sector confidence, and capacity to sustain technological upgrading without excessive reliance on external markets or public support.",

"Europe: combines advanced manufacturing, skilled labor, substantial consumer markets, established institutions, strong positions in selected industrial and specialized technology sectors. Challenge is less absence of economic capacity than difficulty converting capacity into consistently stronger aggregate growth. Fragmented national markets, regulatory complexity, demographic aging, uneven investment constrain productivity and business scaling. Energy costs and external industrial competition affect competitiveness of energy-intensive manufacturing. IMF projects euro-area growth of 1.1% in 2026 and 1.2% in 2027; continued expansion but modest pace relative to needs of economies facing aging populations, higher defense requirements, pressure to invest in energy and industrial transformation. Structural: principal economic challenge is to improve productivity and investment while managing demographic and fiscal constraints. Industrial and institutional strengths remain important, but weak aggregate growth limits resources available for strategic adaptation.",

"India: among fastest-growing major economies, supported by domestic demand, services, infrastructure investment, digital adoption, large labor force. IMF October outlook projects ~7% growth in 2026, well ahead of most major economies in headline terms. Longer-term opportunity: translate growth into sustained productivity improvements, higher-quality employment, expanding household incomes, broader industrial capabilities. Strong GDP growth alone does not establish gains distributed widely or sufficient productive employment created. Infrastructure, education and skills, formal employment, manufacturing competitiveness, participation in global supply chains influence how much demographic and market potential becomes durable economic strength. Structural: substantial growth potential, but long-term position depends on converting rapid expansion into productivity, job creation, and rising living standards at scale.",

"Emerging and lower-income: do not form single macroeconomic category. Commodity exporters, manufacturing hubs, tourism-dependent economies, energy importers, and countries reliant on external financing face very different conditions. Countries integrated into expanding technology and manufacturing supply chains may benefit from investment and export demand. Commodity exporters may receive stronger external revenues when prices rise; import-dependent economies can experience deteriorating trade balances and higher domestic costs. Countries with heavy debt burdens may have less room to protect households or sustain public investment. Latin America and Caribbean: IMF October assessment projects regional growth of 2.3% in 2026 and 2.5% in 2027, while identifying weak productivity growth and elevated public debt as continuing challenges. Structural: external conditions can support growth, but durable convergence requires productivity gains, credible public finances, investment, and stronger domestic productive capacity. Economies with limited fiscal and external buffers remain more exposed to global shocks."
